Chapter 7: Overcoming Cognitive Biases and Mental Shortcuts.
Even when you’re trying your best to think things through, your mind has its own way of taking shortcuts. These mental shortcuts—what psychologists call cognitive biases—are designed to help us make decisions quickly. But as handy as they are, they can just as easily trip us up.
Think about confirmation bias. Ever notice how easy it is to focus on information that backs up what you already believe, while ignoring anything that might prove you wrong? Or maybe you’ve fallen for anchoring, where that very first piece of information you hear sticks in your mind and colors everything else. Then there’s availability bias—where you give more weight to stuff that comes to mind easily, whether it’s actually important or not.
These mental habits are kind of like walking down a familiar path in the woods. It’s comfortable, almost automatic. But sometimes, that path doesn’t actually lead you where you want to go.
So how do you break free and make better choices? Here are a few strategies that really work:
First, try deliberately searching out information that challenges your current point of view. It’s not always fun, but it can really open your eyes.
Next, slow down before making a decision, especially if you’re feeling rushed. Just a short pause can make all the difference.
And if you want a more structured approach, use decision-making tools like checklists or decision matrices. They’ll help you weigh your options more fairly.
Here’s a real-world example: imagine a hiring manager. Without realizing it, they might start favoring candidates who remind them of themselves. But by sticking to a set list of interview questions and clear scoring, the manager can cut down on personal bias—and give everyone a fair shot.
Another trick is to flip the script. Ask yourself: what if I did the exact opposite of what I expect? Or, how would someone from a totally different background see this situation? These questions can help you spot blind spots and discover new possibilities you might’ve missed.
One thing to keep in mind: nobody is immune to bias. Intelligence, experience, none of that makes you bulletproof. The trick isn’t to try to get rid of bias completely—because, honestly, that’s impossible. Instead, it’s about noticing when bias creeps in, and putting up a few guardrails.
Over time, if you can build the habit of asking yourself tough questions and staying humble, you’ll naturally start to catch those mental shortcuts before they lead you off track.
Slow down, challenge your assumptions, and you’ll find yourself making wiser, more creative decisions—ones that just might surprise you.
